  • Years'?
  • The twist ending in "After Twenty Years" intensifies the themes. It highlights the conflict
  • between duty and friendship, adds irony to the theme of change, and enhances the theme of
  • appearance vs. reality, forcing the reader to confront moral complexities.
  • 24 How do the towns people's views on the Happy Prince's statue change over time?
  • Initially, the townspeople admire the Happy Prince statue for its beauty and opulence.
  • However, as the Prince, through the Swallow, starts giving away his jewels and gold to help
  • the poor, they see him as shabby and ultimately order him to be melted down. They value
  • outward appearance and material wealth over compassion and selflessness.
  • 25 What is the central message conveyed through the sacrifices made by the Happy Prince and
  • the Swallow?
  • The Happy Prince and the Swallow sacrifice their beauty and comfort to help the poor and
  • suffering. Their sacrifices convey the central message that true beauty and happiness lie in
  • compassion, selflessness, and love for others, transcending material wealth and appearances.
  • 26 What does the phrase 'a laggard in love, and a dastard in war' imply about the bridegroom?
  • In contrast to Lochinvar, the bridegroom in Sir Walter Scott's poem is indifferent or
  • unpassionate in love and cowardly in war.
  • 27 Describe the relationship between the speaker and Annabel Lee.
  • ● deep and eternal.
  • ● characterized by a love so profound that it was envied by angels in heaven
  • ● Even after Annabel Lee’s death, the speaker remains deeply connected to her.
  • ● Their love continues to transcend the boundaries of life and death.
  • 28 How does the tone of 'The Happy Prince' reflect Wilde’s attitude toward poverty?
  • Wilde uses a melancholic and empathetic tone in "The Happy Prince" to reveal his deep
  • concern for the plight of the poor and marginalized. The story's poignant portrayal of
  • suffering and social injustice reflects Wilde's criticism of societal indifference towards
  • poverty.
  • 29 What does Lochinvar mean when he says, "Love swells like the Solway, but ebbs like its
  • tide"?
  • ● Lochinvar is emphasizing that love, like the tide, can rise powerfully and passionately but
  • can also recede just as quickly, symbolizing its impermanence and unpredictability.
  • ● highlights how love, like nature, can be both beautiful and volatile.
  • 30 What initial feelings does the speaker convey in Sonnet 29, and what circumstances lead to
  • these emotions?
  • ● the speaker initially conveys feelings of deep despair, self-pity, and envy.
  • ● laments his misfortune all alone.
  • ● feels that his cries to heaven go unanswered.
  • ● Shakespeare creates an image of helplessness and frustration

  • He gathers materials like branches; constructs the traps; prepares the rope
  • 34 Describe the concept of gratitude in "The Ape, the Snake and the Lion"
  • When Mvoo Laana shows compassion by releasing the trapped animals, they, in turn, express
  • their gratitude by rewarding him with gifts.
  • a cycle of kindness and appreciation, where good deeds are acknowledged and returned.
  • The story contrasts the animals' gratitude with the ingratitude of the villagers.
  • While the animals appreciate Mvoo Laana's kindness, the villagers are envious of his
  • newfound wealth and ultimately betray him - also subtly questions the motives behind it.

  • overcoming adversity is central to the plot and is presented through a series of escalating
  • challenges that test Little John's courage and resilience.

  • disembodied voices, falling body parts, and a grotesque, reanimating giant.
  • He never shows fear, even when confronted with the most gruesome sights. He eats, drinks
  • and whistles in the face of danger, demonstrating his ability to remain calm under pressure.

  • Setting immediately establishes a sense of danger and suspense- primary location for Little
  • John’s trails and tribulations

  • symbolic language - imagining alternative futures
  • social commentary

  • nature - it leads to his salvation.

questions.question: Identify the cultural tensions depicted in the story “Sacrificial Egg.”
questions.solution_html:
• The story shows cultural identity through Julius’s conflict between his Western education
  • and the traditional Igbo beliefs he witnesses in the market, the rituals, and the sacrificial egg
  • he accidentally steps on. Although he knows such beliefs have no place in rational thinking
  • the later deaths of Ma and Janet—and the empty market he looks out on—force him to
  • confront the community’s traditional explanations and the power those beliefs hold. The
  • story remains relevant because it depicts how individuals still navigate the tension between
  • modern ideas and deeply rooted cultural practices. (, , , )
questions.final_answer: The story shows cultural identity through Julius’s conflict between his Western education

  • symbolic meaning in literature. (, , )

  • environment help readers understand motivations and conflicts. (, , , )

questions.question: What is the stream of consciousness technique?
questions.solution_html:
• Stream of consciousness is a literary technique presenting a character’s continuous flow
  • of thoughts and feelings. It is non-linear, associative, and often fragmented, giving
  • readers direct access to interior consciousness. (, , , )
